name: Ben-hadad
interpretive_note: Many scholars think "Ben-hadad" functioned as a dynastic throne-name for the kings of Aram-Damascus (similar to "Pharaoh" in Egypt) rather than one man's personal name, and that the Ben-hadad who allied with Asa (1 Kings 15) may be a different king -- likely father and son -- from the Ben-hadad who besieged Samaria under Ahab and was later assassinated by his own servant Hazael (1 Kings 20 - 2 Kings 8). Scripture itself does not distinguish two men by name, so this entry follows the text in treating the references as one figure while noting the dispute.
source_summary: A recurring king of Aram-Damascus during Israel's divided monarchy, allied against and at war with Israel across the reigns of Asa, Baasha, and Ahab, whose armies besieged Samaria twice and who was eventually assassinated by his own servant Hazael.
family_friendly_summary: Ben-hadad was a powerful king of Aram (Syria) who fought against Israel again and again during the time of Kings Asa and Ahab. At first, Judah's King Asa paid him to attack Israel's northern border. Later, Ben-hadad surrounded Israel's capital city with a huge army and demanded that King Ahab give up his treasures and his family -- but Ahab refused, and God gave Israel a surprising victory even though Ben-hadad's army was much bigger. Ahab showed him mercy and let him go free. Ben-hadad's soldiers also tried to capture the prophet Elisha, who kept warning Israel about Aram's war plans, but God protected Elisha instead. Ben-hadad's story shows that no army is too strong for God to overcome when He chooses to protect His people.
adult_story: Ben-hadad, son of Tabrimmon, ruled Aram from Damascus during Israel's divided-monarchy wars, appearing across the reigns of Asa, Baasha, and Ahab (many scholars think "Ben-hadad" names father and son bearing a shared dynastic title, not one long-reigning man -- see note). Judah's King Asa bribed him with temple treasure to break his alliance with Baasha and attack Israel instead (1 Kings 15:18-20; 2 Chronicles 16:2-7) -- a move the prophet Hanani condemned as trusting Aram instead of the LORD. Later, besieging Samaria with thirty-two allied kings, Ben-hadad arrogantly demanded Ahab's wives and children, then, boasting drunk in his tent, was routed by a small Israelite force; the next year he returned with a valley army, confident Israel's God only ruled hills, and was crushed again (1 Kings 20). Ahab spared him and made a covenant, drawing a prophet's rebuke for releasing a man devoted to destruction. Ben-hadad's officers later hunted Elisha for exposing his battle plans, only for God to blind the search party and for Elisha to feed and release them (2 Kings 6:8-23); he then besieged Samaria himself, starving the city (6:24). Finally, sick in Damascus, he sent his servant Hazael to ask Elisha whether he would recover -- not knowing Hazael would soon smother him and seize his throne (2 Kings 8:7-9).

devotionals: Ben-hadad sent his own servant to ask Elisha about his fate, never expecting that servant to kill him. Jesus alone holds every person's future, unlike any human plan.
Ahab spared Ben-hadad against God's command, and a prophet warned that misapplied mercy still carries a cost. Jesus offers mercy that satisfies God's justice rather than ignoring it.
